newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish strife rumbles on under peace veneer.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish strife rumbles on under peace veneer.

text.p: On the road into Ballymena, trees are plastered with orange posters demanding "Are You Guilty In God's Eyes?"
This is Northern Ireland's Bible belt and the colour orange is an unmistakable declaration; this is Protestant territory.

In Harryville, one of Ballymena's poorer suburbs, Catholics make up just two percent of the population and in the past few weeks they have become the target of intimidation and sometimes vicious attacks by Protestant extremists.
The trouble began in September when Protestant marchers were banned from parading through the Catholic village of Dunloy, some 15 miles (25 km) from Ballymena.
Protestants were outraged. Each Saturday since then, hundreds have gathered outside Harryville's Church of Our Lady each Saturday to try to stop Catholics from attending mass.
They hurl fireworks and abuse and sing Protestant songs.
One woman was dragged from her car and beaten and several Catholic homes in Harryville have been firebombed.
"It is very intimidating," said Canon Sean Connolly, of Our Lady's church. "The congregation sits in the church listening to the chanting knowing they have to go out and face it again."

Protestant guerrillas called a truce in Northern Ireland over two years ago and although their Irish Republican Army (IRA) rivals abandoned their ceasefire in February, they have carried out only one bombing in the province so far.

Despite this veneer of peace, sectarian problems have rumbled on and when the annual marching season by local lodges of the Protestant Orange Order began in July, long-harboured grievances exploded into violence.
To many Catholics who want a united Ireland, the marchers with their bowler hats, orange sashes and huge drums, are triumphing in Britain's continuing rule of the province.
Seeing clashes looming, police banned or diverted many of the marches so that they would not pass through Catholic areas.
But this only provoked Protestants and the province suffered its worst period of violence for years.
In Drumcree, south of Belfast, riots broke out after police first banned an Orange march and then allowed it to go ahead. The damage cost 40 million pounds ($66 million).

It was largely due to this escalation in sectarian conflict that Britain's minister for Northern Ireland, Sir Patrick Mayhew, announced this week he was boosting spending on security in the province by 120 million pounds ($200 million) for the next three years.
Security costs had been cut after the ceasefires.
Ballymena's Protestant council leaders are keen to stress that sectarian problems are rare in their prosperous town.
"The problems in Harryville came out of the blue," Mayor James Currie told Reuters.
Currie has condemned the attacks and he and his fellow councillors joined a vigil outside the church last weekend which helped subdue the protestors.
Even so, Our Lady's church, an angular, copper-roofed 1960's building, has had a spiked steel fence and metal grilles over its windows for many years.
On July 12, the day Protestants celebrate a 17th century victory over a Catholic king, the priest's house beside the church was firebombed.
"These attacks have been pretty routine over the years, although they have never been this bad," said Canon Connolly.
